questions.answer: Which game would you like to play at recess: soccer, kickball, tag or jump rope?
questions.solution: A good question asks about the topic and offers choices that can be counted. "Do you like games?" does not show which game, and the last question is about something else.

solve.answer: Which game would you like to play at recess: soccer, kickball, tag or jump rope?
solve.work: Best question is unbiased, on topic, with clear choices: the list of recess games.

questions.skill: Pose a question that data can answer
questions.stem: Lia wants to find out how the students in her class get to school. Which question should she ask so the answers are easy to put in a frequency table?
choices: Why do you get to school?
How do you get to school: walk, bike, bus or car?
What time do you get to school?
questions.answer: How do you get to school: walk, bike, bus or car?
questions.solution: This question gives a few categories that Lia can tally. The other questions do not tell how students get to school.

solve.answer: How do you get to school: walk, bike, bus or car?
solve.work: Giving the categories walk, bike, bus, car makes a frequency table easy.

questions.skill: Plan and carry out data collection
questions.stem: Ben asked his class which sport they like best and wrote down every answer. What should he do next?
choices: Write his conclusion before looking at any data
Put the answers in a table or graph
questions.answer: Put the answers in a table or graph
questions.solution: After collecting data, the next step is to organize it in a frequency table or graph so it is easy to read. Then he can draw conclusions.

solve.answer: Put the answers in a table or graph
solve.work: After collecting, organize the data in a table or graph.

questions.skill: Plan and carry out data collection
questions.stem: Jo plans to ask 24 students for their favorite fruit. So far she has tallied 9 votes for apples, 7 for bananas and 5 for pears. How many more students does she still need to ask?
questions.solution: She has asked $9 + 7 + 5 = 21$ students. She still needs to ask $24 - 21 = 3$ students.

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: A frequency table shows the pets of 30 students: dog 12, cat 9, fish 5 and bird 4. Which statement is true?
choices: Dogs are the most common pet
Fish and birds together are the most common pet
Cats are the least common pet
questions.answer: Dogs are the most common pet
questions.solution: Dog has the greatest number, 12. Fish and birds together make 9, which is less than 12. Birds are the least common, not cats. The table does not tell about students with no pet.

solve.answer: Dogs are the most common pet
solve.work: Dogs 12 is most. Fish + birds 9 < 12; cats 9 not least (bird 4); 12 + 9 + 5 + 4 = 30 so nobody lacks a pet.

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: A bar graph shows how students get to school: bus 24, walk 12, car 16 and bike 4. Which statement is NOT supported by the graph?
choices: Twice as many students ride the bus as walk
More students come by car than by bike
More students walk than come by car
Bike is the least common way to get to school
questions.answer: More students walk than come by car
questions.solution: Walk is 12 and car is 16, so more students come by car than walk. The other three statements match the graph.

solve.answer: More students walk than come by car
solve.work: Bike 4 least: supported. Bus 24 = 2 x walk 12: supported. Walk 12 < car 16, so 'more walk than car' is NOT supported. Car 16 > bike 4: supported.

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: A bar graph shows how many students bought lunch: Monday 20, Tuesday 22, Wednesday 24 and Thursday 26. If the pattern continues, how many students will probably buy lunch on Friday?
questions.solution: The numbers go up by 2 each day, so Friday will probably be $26 + 2 = 28$.

questions.skill: Picture graph with a half symbol
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each smiley face stands for 6 students. The row for art has 3 whole smiley faces and 1 half smiley face. How many students does the art row stand for?
questions.solution: 3 whole faces: $3 \times 6 = 18$ students. A half face is half of 6, which is 3 students. Total: 18 + 3 = 21 students.

questions.skill: Draw a conclusion from a frequency table
questions.stem: A class made a frequency table of how students get to school: walk 12, bus 18, car 8, bike 2. Which statement is supported by the data?
choices: More students walk than ride the bus.
Exactly half of the students ride the bus.
More students ride the bus than walk.
questions.answer: More students ride the bus than walk.
questions.solution: The bus has 18 and walking has 12, so more students ride the bus. Bike has the fewest (2). The class has 12 + 18 + 8 + 2 = 40 students, and half of 40 is 20, not 18.

solve.answer: More students ride the bus than walk.
solve.work: Bus 18 > walk 12, so more ride the bus than walk (true). Bike 2 is fewest; total 40, half is 20, bus is 18, not half.

questions.skill: Read and use a frequency table
questions.stem: 50 students voted for an ice cream flavor. A frequency table shows vanilla 15, chocolate 12 and strawberry 9. The rest of the students chose mint. How many more students chose vanilla than mint?
questions.solution: Vanilla, chocolate and strawberry total $15 + 12 + 9 = 36$ votes, so mint got $50 - 36 = 14$ votes. Vanilla got $15 - 14 = 1$ more vote than mint.

questions.skill: Read and use a frequency table
questions.stem: A bakery table shows how many cookies were sold: oatmeal 18, chocolate chip 27 and sugar 15. The bakery also sold 4 more peanut butter cookies than sugar cookies. How many cookies were sold in all?
questions.solution: Peanut butter cookies sold: $15 + 4 = 19$. Total: $18 + 27 + 15 + 19 = 79$ cookies.

questions.skill: Read and use a frequency table
questions.stem: A frequency table shows votes for a class pet: hamster 13, rabbit 9, turtle 13 and gecko 7. Which statement is NOT true?
choices: Hamster got more votes than any other pet
Rabbit got more votes than gecko
Hamster and turtle got the same number of votes
questions.answer: Hamster got more votes than any other pet
questions.solution: Hamster and turtle each got 13 votes, so hamster did not get more votes than every other pet. The other three statements are true.

solve.answer: Hamster got more votes than any other pet
solve.work: Gecko 7 fewest: true. Rabbit 9 > gecko 7: true. Hamster 13 ties turtle 13, so 'more than any other' is false. Hamster = turtle: true.

questions.skill: Tally marks and organizing a list of answers
questions.stem: A tally chart shows how many books were returned each day. Monday: 2 full groups of five and 1 mark. Tuesday: 1 full group and 4 marks. Wednesday: 3 full groups. Thursday: 2 full groups and 2 marks. Friday: 1 full group and 3 marks. How many books were returned in all?
questions.solution: Monday 11, Tuesday 9, Wednesday 15, Thursday 12 and Friday 8. Add them: $11 + 9 + 15 + 12 + 8 = 55$ books.

questions.skill: Tally marks and organizing a list of answers
questions.stem: Fifteen students named their favorite fruit: apple, grape, apple, pear, grape, apple, apple, pear, grape, apple, pear, grape, apple, apple, grape. How many more students chose apple than pear?
questions.solution: Count each fruit: apple 7 times, grape 5 times, pear 3 times (they total 15). Apple has $7 - 3 = 4$ more than pear.

questions.skill: Read a scaled bar graph
questions.stem: A bar graph's scale counts by 10s. The bar for walk ends halfway between 30 and 40. The bar for bike ends halfway between 10 and 20. How many more students walk than bike?
questions.solution: Halfway between 30 and 40 is 35, and halfway between 10 and 20 is 15. The difference is $35 - 15 = 20$ students.

questions.skill: Read a scaled bar graph
questions.stem: A bar graph's scale counts by 5s. It shows pages read: Ana's bar ends at 35, Ben's at 20 and Cy's at 25. Dee read as many pages as Ben and Cy together. At what number does Dee's bar end?
questions.solution: Dee read $20 + 25 = 45$ pages, so her bar ends at 45.

questions.skill: Read a picture graph with a key
questions.stem: A picture graph uses 1 picture for every 2 students. Mr. Lin redraws it so that 1 picture stands for 6 students. 24 students chose swimming. How many fewer pictures show swimming in the new graph than in the old graph?
questions.solution: Old graph: $24 \div 2 = 12$ pictures. New graph: $24 \div 6 = 4$ pictures. That is $12 - 4 = 8$ fewer pictures.

questions.skill: Read a picture graph with a key
questions.stem: In Graph 1, each picture stands for 10 students, and Row A has 3 pictures. In Graph 2, each picture stands for 5 students, and Row B has 5 pictures. Which statement is true?
choices: Row B stands for more students because it has more pictures
Row A stands for more students than Row B
The two rows stand for the same number of students
questions.answer: Row A stands for more students than Row B
questions.solution: Row A stands for $3 \times 10 = 30$ students and Row B stands for $5 \times 5 = 25$ students. Row A stands for more, even though it has fewer pictures.

solve.answer: Row A stands for more students than Row B
solve.work: Row A: 3 x 10 = 30. Row B: 5 x 5 = 25. A stands for more.

questions.skill: Read a picture graph with a key
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each sun stands for 4 sunny days and half a sun stands for 2 days. May's row has 3 whole suns and 1 half sun. June's row has 2 whole suns. How many more sunny days did May have than June?
questions.solution: May: $3 \times 4 + 2 = 14$ days. June: $2 \times 4 = 8$ days. May had $14 - 8 = 6$ more sunny days.

questions.skill: Read a picture graph with a key
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 3 pictures, Tuesday has 5 pictures, Wednesday has 2 pictures, and Thursday has some pictures. The four rows stand for 60 books in all. How many pictures are in Thursday's row?
questions.solution: The 60 books are $60 \div 5 = 12$ pictures in all. Monday to Wednesday use $3 + 5 + 2 = 10$ pictures, so Thursday has $12 - 10 = 2$ pictures.

questions.skill: Compare categories: how many more or fewer
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each picture stands for 4 students and half a picture stands for 2 students. The dog row has 9 whole pictures. The cat row has 6 whole pictures and 1 half picture. How many more students chose dogs than cats?
questions.solution: Dogs: $9 \times 4 = 36$ students. Cats: $6 \times 4 + 2 = 26$ students. Dogs got $36 - 26 = 10$ more.

questions.skill: Compare categories: how many more or fewer
questions.stem: Two classes voted for a color. Class A: red 12, blue 9, green 14. Class B: red 10, blue 15, green 8. For which color did Class B get more votes than Class A?
questions.solution: Compare each color. Red: 10 is less than 12. Blue: 15 is more than 9. Green: 8 is less than 14. Only blue had more votes in Class B.

questions.skill: Compare categories: how many more or fewer
questions.stem: A bar graph's scale counts by 20s. The bars end at 60 for Monday, 100 for Tuesday and 80 for Wednesday. Thursday's bar is 20 shorter than Monday's bar. How many fewer does Thursday show than Tuesday?
questions.solution: Thursday shows $60 - 20 = 40$. Tuesday shows 100. The difference is $100 - 40 = 60$ fewer.

questions.skill: Two-step problems from a graph or table
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each picture stands for 3 students. The dog row has 9 pictures, the cat row has 6 pictures and the fish row has 2 pictures. How many more students chose dogs than chose cats and fish together?
questions.solution: Dogs: $9 \times 3 = 27$. Cats and fish: $6 \times 3 + 2 \times 3 = 18 + 6 = 24$. The difference is $27 - 24 = 3$ students.

questions.skill: Two-step problems from a graph or table
questions.stem: A bar graph's scale counts by 4s. The bars show books read by four teams: Reds 24, Blues 16, Greens 20 and Yellows 12. The two teams that read the most books are joined into one team. How many books did the joined team read?
questions.solution: The two highest bars are Reds (24) and Greens (20). Joined: $24 + 20 = 44$ books.

questions.skill: Two-step problems from a graph or table
questions.stem: A bar graph shows the number of students who bought lunch: Monday 40, Tuesday 20, Wednesday 60 and Thursday 30. Which statement is true?
choices: Thursday had twice as many students as Tuesday
Wednesday had 30 more students than Monday
Tuesday had half as many students as Wednesday
Wednesday had as many students as Monday and Tuesday together
questions.answer: Wednesday had as many students as Monday and Tuesday together
questions.solution: Monday and Tuesday together: $40 + 20 = 60$, the same as Wednesday. Twice Tuesday is 40, not 30. Wednesday is $60 - 40 = 20$ more than Monday, not 30. Half of Wednesday is 30, not 20.

solve.answer: Wednesday had as many students as Monday and Tuesday together
solve.work: Thu 30 vs Tue 20: not twice. Wed 60 - Mon 40 = 20, not 30. Mon + Tue = 60 = Wed: true. Tue 20 is a third of Wed 60, not half.

questions.skill: Two-step problems from a graph or table
questions.stem: A bar graph's scale counts by 5s. It shows sit-ups: Monday 15, Tuesday 25 and Wednesday 20. On Thursday Mia does as many sit-ups as on Monday and Tuesday together. On Friday she does 5 fewer than on Thursday. How many sit-ups does she do on Friday?
questions.solution: Thursday: $15 + 25 = 40$ sit-ups. Friday: $40 - 5 = 35$ sit-ups.

questions.skill: Make a graph: choose a scale or the number of symbols
questions.stem: Mia draws a picture graph in which each picture stands for 9 students. Three rows need to show 18 students, 27 students and 36 students. How many pictures does she draw in all?
questions.solution: The rows need $18 \div 9 = 2$, $27 \div 9 = 3$ and $36 \div 9 = 4$ pictures. In all: $2 + 3 + 4 = 9$ pictures.

questions.skill: Make a graph: choose a scale or the number of symbols
questions.stem: Zoe's data are 12, 18, 30 and 24. Which bar graph scale lands exactly on every one of these numbers?
questions.solution: All four numbers are multiples of 6, so counting by 6s (6, 12, 18, 24, 30) lands on all of them. 18 is not a multiple of 4, 12 is not a multiple of 5, and 12 is not a multiple of 8.

solve.work: 12, 18, 24, 30 are all multiples of 6. By 4s misses 18, 30; by 8s misses 12, 18, 30; by 5s misses 12, 18, 24.

questions.skill: Make a graph: choose a scale or the number of symbols
questions.stem: Tess makes a bar graph with a scale that counts by 5s. Her data are 15 for football, 25 for basketball and 10 for baseball. How many lines taller is the basketball bar than the baseball bar?
questions.solution: The basketball bar is $25 \div 5 = 5$ lines tall and the baseball bar is $10 \div 5 = 2$ lines tall. The basketball bar is $5 - 2 = 3$ lines taller.

questions.skill: Pose a question that data can answer
questions.stem: Which question is a fair way to find out the class's favorite pizza topping?
choices: Which topping do you like best: cheese, pepperoni or mushroom?
Don't you agree that pepperoni is the best topping?
What toppings does your mom like?
questions.answer: Which topping do you like best: cheese, pepperoni or mushroom?
questions.solution: A fair question does not push people toward one answer. "Don't you agree that pepperoni is the best topping?" pushes toward pepperoni, asking what your mom likes asks about someone else, and "Do you eat pizza?" does not ask about toppings.

solve.answer: Which topping do you like best: cheese, pepperoni or mushroom?
solve.work: Fair = asks the student's own preference, not leading: the choice of three toppings.

questions.skill: Pose a question that data can answer
questions.stem: Which question would give different answers from different students, so collecting data makes sense?
choices: How many days are in a week?
How many sides does a triangle have?
How many brothers and sisters does each student in our class have?
questions.answer: How many brothers and sisters does each student in our class have?
questions.solution: Students can have different numbers of brothers and sisters, so data is needed. The other questions have the same answer for everyone.

solve.answer: How many brothers and sisters does each student in our class have?
solve.work: Only the number of siblings varies from student to student; the others have one fixed answer.

questions.skill: Plan and carry out data collection
questions.stem: Ken wants to find out what third graders eat for breakfast. Which set of categories for his table has a place for every answer and no overlap?
choices: cereal, cereal with milk, eggs, toast
questions.solution: Good categories let every answer fit in exactly one row. "Something else" catches other answers. Cereal and cereal with milk overlap, and "breakfast" overlaps with everything. The list with only cereal and eggs has no row for toast.

solve.work: 'something else' catches every other answer and the four categories do not overlap. Others overlap (cereal / cereal with milk; breakfast) or leave answers out.

questions.skill: Plan and carry out data collection
questions.stem: Anna and Ben each want to find the favorite sport of all third graders at their school. Anna asks the 5 students on the soccer team. Ben asks every third grader to pick a sport from a list. Whose plan is better?
choices: Anna's, because soccer players know sports
Anna's, because she asks fewer students
Ben's, because he asks all the third graders
questions.answer: Ben's, because he asks all the third graders
questions.solution: Ben asks the whole group he wants to know about. Anna only asks soccer players, so her results may not show what all third graders think.

solve.answer: Ben's, because he asks all the third graders
solve.work: Asking all third graders represents the whole group; soccer players are biased.

questions.skill: Plan and carry out data collection
questions.stem: A class makes a tally chart of pets with rows for dog, cat, fish and bird. One student has a rabbit. What is the best fix for the chart?
choices: Count the rabbit as a cat
Add a row for rabbit or other
questions.answer: Add a row for rabbit or other
questions.solution: Every answer should have a row of its own. Adding a row for rabbit (or other) keeps the data true.

solve.answer: Add a row for rabbit or other
solve.work: Every answer needs a place: add a rabbit (or other) row.

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: Sam asked 10 students at the soccer field which sport they like best. Nine said soccer. Sam says, "Most students in our school like soccer best." What is wrong with his conclusion?
choices: Nine is too small a number
He asked only students at the soccer field, so his data may not show the whole school
He should have asked fewer students
questions.answer: He asked only students at the soccer field, so his data may not show the whole school
questions.solution: Students at the soccer field are more likely to like soccer. Sam did not ask a fair group of the whole school, so he cannot conclude this about all students.

solve.answer: He asked only students at the soccer field, so his data may not show the whole school
solve.work: The sample (students at the soccer field) is biased and not the whole school.

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 pictures and Wednesday has 8 pictures. If the pattern continues, how many books will Thursday's row stand for?
questions.solution: The number of pictures goes up by 2 each day: 4, 6, 8, so Thursday will probably have 10 pictures. Ten pictures stand for $10 \times 5 = 50$ books.

solve.work: Pictures 4, 6, 8 grow by 2, so Thursday 10 pictures = 50 books (books 20, 30, 40, 50).

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: A bar graph shows votes for a favorite season: spring 7, summer 14, fall 9 and winter 6. Which statement is true?
choices: Fall got twice as many votes as winter
Winter and spring together got more votes than summer
Summer got 7 more votes than fall
Summer got twice as many votes as spring
questions.answer: Summer got twice as many votes as spring
questions.solution: 14 is twice 7. Twice winter is 12, not 9. Winter and spring together make 13, which is less than 14. Summer is $14 - 9 = 5$ more than fall, not 7.

solve.answer: Summer got twice as many votes as spring
solve.work: Summer - fall = 5, not 7. Summer 14 = 2 x spring 7: true. Fall 9 is not 2 x 6. Winter + spring = 13 < 14.

questions.skill: Draw conclusions and make predictions from data
questions.stem: A bar graph shows how many students chose each lunch: pizza 18, salad 7 and sandwich 11. Which question can NOT be answered by looking at the graph?
choices: How many more students chose pizza than salad?
Which lunch did the fewest students choose?
Why did so many students choose pizza?
How many students chose a lunch in all?
questions.answer: Why did so many students choose pizza?
questions.solution: The graph shows how many chose each lunch, but not the reasons. The other questions can be answered with the numbers on the graph.

solve.answer: Why did so many students choose pizza?
solve.work: The graph gives counts, not reasons: 'Why...' cannot be answered. Total (36), difference (11) and fewest (salad) can.

questions.skill: Show a number of students with whole and half symbols
questions.stem: In a picture graph, each circle stands for 8 students, and half a circle stands for 4 students. 28 students chose art. Which shows the row for art?
questions.solution: Each whole circle is 8 students. 3 whole circles are 3 x 8 = 24 students, and 28 - 24 = 4 students are left. 4 students is exactly 1 half circle. So the row has 3 whole circles and 1 half circle.

solve.work: 28 / 8 = 3 remainder 4, so 3 whole circles (24) and 1 half circle (4) = 28. Others: 4 whole = 32; 7 whole = 56; 3 whole + 2 halves = 24 + 8 = 32. Only one option equals 28.
